title: Achromatism and Its Applications
notes: An optical pair is achromatic for two chosen colours when their wavelength-dependent deviations cancel and both colours share a final focus. The lenses remain dispersive individually; their effects compensate.

For two thin lenses in contact with signed focal lengths f1,f2 and dispersive powers ω1,ω2, primary achromatism requires ω1/f1+ω2/f2=0. A crown converging lens is commonly paired with a more dispersive flint diverging lens.
Worked design: f1=+20 cm, ω1=0.02 and ω2=0.04 require 0.02/20+0.04/f2=0, giving f2=−40 cm. The negative sign identifies a diverging flint element.
The net power is 1/F=1/f1+1/f2, so the doublet can remain converging while cancelling colour spread. Camera, telescope and microscope objectives use achromatic groups to reduce coloured fringes.
Primary achromatism corrects two selected wavelengths; other colours may still form a secondary spectrum. More elaborate apochromatic systems correct additional wavelengths.

Two thin lenses in contact are achromatic for the mean colours when ω1/f1 + ω2/f2 = 0. The flint lens has the higher dispersive power, so it can cancel the colour of a stronger crown lens even though its own power is smaller. The combination still converges.

specificConditions: **Dispersion Definition:** Dispersion is the separation of white light into its constituent colors (spectrum) due to the dependence of the refractive index $n$ on the wavelength $\lambda$ of light ($n(\lambda)$).

**Cauchy's Equation:** For many transparent materials, the refractive index follows Cauchy's equation $n(\lambda) = A + B/\lambda^2 + C/\lambda^4$. This explains why blue light ($\lambda$ smaller) is refracted more than red light ($\lambda$ larger).

**Prism Validity:** The formula for dispersive power $\omega = (n_v - n_r)/(n_y - 1)$ assumes small angle of deviation and that the prism is in air. For non-thin prisms or different mediums, angular dispersion depends on the geometry.
